item.title: OpenAI releases massive collection of AI‑generated mathematical results
item.description:
OpenAI releases massive collection of AI‑generated mathematical results

OpenAI has published a large repository of AI‑generated mathematics, prompting an immediate response from the research community.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI released nearly 400 AI‑generated results.
  • The results are spread across more than 700 manuscripts (719 manuscripts mentioned on GitHub).
  • The collection covers a wide range of mathematical fields, including combinatorics, geometry, number theory, theoretical computer science, algebra, topology, probability, statistical mechanics, and mathematical physics.
  • OpenAI published guidance to help users navigate the sprawling GitHub repository.

📚 Scope of the Release

  • Manuscripts: >700 (exactly 719 mentioned).
  • AI‑generated results: ~400.
  • Table of contents: Roughly 40‑page list of abstracts.
  • Disciplines covered: combinatorics, several branches of geometry, number theory, theoretical computer science, algebra, topology, probability and statistical mechanics, mathematical physics.

🛠️ Formal Verification Status

  • Many manuscripts contain formalizations in Lean, a proof assistant that allows computational verification.
  • OpenAI notes the results are “at different stages of verification” and that “many, but not all, of the manuscripts have been formalized.”
  • 300 top‑line results out of 719 manuscripts have been formalized (around 42 percent).
  • As of writing, fewer than half the manuscripts appear to have been described formally.
  • Researchers must check that a formalization actually proves what the result claims, a time‑consuming process.
  • The quality was inconsistent and the statements verified did not always map neatly onto the claims in accompanying manuscripts.
Metric Value
AI‑generated results nearly 400
Total manuscripts 719
Formalized top‑line results 300 (≈42 %)
Formalized manuscripts fewer than half

😕 Community Reaction

“Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop”

“Just going over the entire list of abstracts is overwhelming,” said Álvaro Lozano‑Robledo, a professor of mathematics at the University of Connecticut.

“Hence, I either have to read possibly‑not‑correct slop, or wait for others to do the same, or wait for someone to formalise them before I can say for sure that the results are even correct.”

“It’s a big mess. It can cause a huge collapse in the academic culture and simply kill most of the faculties. It’s a social problem and it seems that the AI labs are completely ignoring this issue.”

  • Several researchers have dubbed the flood of papers the “slopocalypse.”
  • Kevin Buzzard (Imperial College London) identified “numerous theorems” in his area (algebraic number theory) but only around six immediately “stood out,” and few seemed formally verified in Lean.
  • Mathematicians reported that working through the 40‑page table of contents and abstracts took “the better part of an hour.”
  • Some fear OpenAI may release even more work before the community can fully assess the current batch.

📍 What’s Next

  • OpenAI said it “will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them.”
  • The guidance published on GitHub aims to help researchers navigate the collection despite its size and varying verification status.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIresearch

Source: ‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop

item.title: OpenAI publishes frontier-model generated mathematical results on GitHub
item.description:
OpenAI publishes frontier-model generated mathematical results on GitHub

OpenAI has made public a collection of new mathematical results generated by an internal frontier model, releasing the data and artifacts for the research community.

🔍 Overview

  • An internal frontier model at OpenAI produced a broad range of new mathematical results.
  • The findings are shared in a public GitHub repository.
  • Advice from the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study was incorporated.

🧩 What’s Included

  • Lean proof formalizations for each result.
  • Summaries that capture the reasoning steps behind the proofs.
  • Compute estimates that detail the resources used to obtain each result.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The repository centralizes formal proofs, reasoning documentation, and compute metadata.
  • Collaboration with the Advisory Group ensures the release aligns with expert recommendations on mathematical AI research.

🚀 Availability

  • All materials are openly accessible via the GitHub repository announced by OpenAI.
  • Researchers can clone the repo, explore the Lean formalizations, and review the compute estimates.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Providing formalized proofs and compute budgets supports reproducibility and transparency in AI‑driven mathematics.
  • The release offers a concrete benchmark for future frontier models attempting mathematical discovery.
  • Community access encourages independent verification and further development of AI‑assisted proof techniques.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIResearch

item.title: OpenAI releases 722 manuscripts solving hundreds of longstanding math problems
item.description:
OpenAI releases 722 manuscripts solving hundreds of longstanding math problems

OpenAI has made public a new batch of mathematical results generated by an unreleased frontier model. The release contains 722 manuscripts that together address 372 families of related problems, offering solutions to hundreds of open questions in mathematics.

🔍 Overview

  • The batch follows earlier announcements that the model had resolved more than 100 open problems across most areas of mathematics.
  • The community has reacted with both admiration for the speed of discovery and concern over research ethics and academic conduct.

📜 What was released

  • 722 manuscripts covering 372 result families that group related papers.
  • The manuscripts include summaries of the model’s reasoning, compute estimates, and statistics on the number of problems attempted.
  • OpenAI states that the “average result” used the equivalent of three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

⚙️ Technical details

Metric Value
Manuscripts released 722
Result families 372
Compute per average result ≈ 3 hours of ChatGPT Pro

The papers are hosted in a GitHub repository, with protocols for revisions and citations. OpenAI says it is exploring other community‑hosted alternatives that meet the advisory committee’s guidelines.

🧭 Community and ethics response

  • The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), an independent group of elite mathematicians, notes that the release includes solutions to “hundreds” of open questions.
  • In late September, AGMAI issued recommendations urging AI labs to publish mathematical results promptly through established academic channels, disclosing model name, prompts, and compute costs.
  • AGMAI also urged companies to avoid using result releases as marketing tools, citing the potential harm to the mathematical community.

📈 Next steps / impact

  • The full impact will become clearer as mathematicians assess and digest the results.
  • These findings add to a rapidly growing body of AI‑generated mathematics that also includes work on a Millennium Prize problem and contributions from rival labs such as Anthropic.
  • Ongoing debate focuses on research practices, ethical considerations, and proper credit for human mathematicians whose work underlies the AI‑generated proofs.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIResearch #AcademicEthics

Source: OpenAI drops another batch of mathematical breakthroughs

item.title: OpenAI Announces Navier‑Stokes Solution and Forms Advisory Panel Amid Backlash
item.description:
OpenAI Announces Navier‑Stokes Solution and Forms Advisory Panel Amid Backlash

OpenAI announced that its internal AI model has produced a solution to the Navier‑Stokes Millennium Prize problem, and the company responded to the ensuing controversy by creating an independent advisory panel of elite mathematicians.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem – the Navier‑Stokes problem, a challenge unsolved for around 90 years.
  • The breakthrough was presented in a blog post on a Tuesday and described as an achievement that demonstrates how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
  • The announcement sparked immediate backlash from the mathematical community, raising concerns about academic norms, credit, and the motivations behind the work.

⚙️ What OpenAI announced

  • The solution was generated by an internal AI model that the company said is “more powerful than the newly re…”.
  • OpenAI framed the result as a historic achievement, noting that such a discovery would normally be celebrated.

📣 Community reaction

  • Mathematicians voiced unease, describing OpenAI as an “impossibly well‑resourced interloper” that appears to be driven by winning rather than advancing the field.
  • Accusations surfaced of scooping, spying, and violating long‑standing academic norms, which some fear could have a chilling effect on research.
  • Andreas Thom raised concerns that prior interactions with the ChatGPT chatbot may have contributed to the success, and OpenAI acknowledged that the result built heavily on his and Gábor Kun’s earlier work.
  • A second mathematician accused OpenAI of “unethical and dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data.
  • Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explained that OpenAI has engaged in “the kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.”

🤝 OpenAI’s response

  • OpenAI announced a new independent panel of elite mathematicians tasked with advising the company and other AI firms on how to interact with mathematical research and the wider community.
  • The panel’s formation “caught many mathematicians by surprise,” and researchers questioned what the group will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will heed its advice.
  • The first assignment for the panel is to help coordinate the release of scores of additional results that OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, a prospect that has already stirred dread among researchers.

📈 Why it matters

  • The episode illustrates the tension between rapid AI‑driven discoveries and established scholarly practices.
  • How OpenAI manages the release of AI‑generated mathematics could shape future collaborations—or conflicts—between industry and the academic community.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIResearch #MillenniumPrize

Source: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics

item.title: Mathematicians form independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Mathematicians form independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence

On September 21st, a group of elite mathematicians announced the formation of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) via a guest post on the blog of UCLA professor and Fields Medalist Terence Tao.

🔍 Overview

AGMAI is an independent body composed of nine mathematicians at the top of their field. The group’s purpose is to advise OpenAI and other frontier AI labs on the “review and communication of emerging results.”

⚙️ Key details

  • Formation: The group formed after OpenAI approached some eventual members about an advisory board; the members subsequently decided to strike out independently and invite others to join.
  • Independence: Martin Hairer, a professor at Imperial College London and EPFL, stated the group receives no financial, technical, or other support from OpenAI and that members are not paid by the company.
  • Governance: Members have not signed agreements restricting their actions or speech, beyond standard confidentiality requirements necessary for advanced research access.
  • Scope: OpenAI noted that AGMAI will not be responsible for advising the company on how to pace internal progress on mathematics.
  • Collaboration: The group is open to working with other frontier AI labs and has already begun conversations with some.

💡 Why it matters

The formation of the group follows a period of community suspicion after OpenAI’s solution to a Millennium Prize problem led to disputes over scooping, credit, and the treatment of mathematicians. Since solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, OpenAI claims an unreleased internal model has resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems.

#AGMAI #OpenAI #Mathematics #AIResearch

Source: OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians

item.title: New Tail-Aware Geometry Learning Framework for Multivariate Conformal Prediction
item.description:
New Tail-Aware Geometry Learning Framework for Multivariate Conformal Prediction

Researchers have introduced a tail-aware geometry learning framework for conformal ellipsoids to improve uncertainty quantification in multivariate conformal prediction (CP).

🔍 Overview

Multivariate conformal prediction is a distribution-free uncertainty quantification framework providing finite-sample coverage guarantees. This new approach addresses limitations in existing minimum-volume methods, which rely on quantile thresholds that ignore tail residual severity and bind geometry learning to coverage levels.

🧩 How it works

The proposed framework decouples tail sensitivity in geometry learning from the final coverage guarantee using the following process:

  • Two-split design: The system uses an estimation split and a held-out calibration split.
  • Metric matrix learning: The metric matrix is learned via volume minimization under a CVaR constraint on the estimation split.
  • Calibration: Standard conformal calibration is applied to the held-out calibration split.

⚙️ Key details

  • Convexity: The resulting problem is convex.
  • Bounded-reweighting: The method admits a bounded-reweighting interpretation that prioritizes samples with high residuals.
  • Theoretical characterization: The research characterizes the trade-off between ellipsoidal volume and tail severity.
  • Performance: Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.

#ConformalPrediction #UncertaintyQuantification #MachineLearning #MultivariateAnalysis

Source: Tail-Aware Geometry Learning for Conformal Ellipsoids

item.title: OpenAI Solves Navier-Stokes Problem Amid Controversy With Mathematicians
item.description:
OpenAI Solves Navier-Stokes Problem Amid Controversy With Mathematicians

OpenAI has announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems established by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. The development has been accompanied by disputes involving NYU professor Tristan Buckmaster regarding the company’s conduct and the use of researcher data.

⚙️ Key details

OpenAI utilized an advanced, unreleased model to find the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. The process involved:

  • Compute resources: Tens of millions of dollars of compute.
  • Agent scale: Roughly 10,000 agents.
  • Timeframe: 88 hours.

🔍 Overview

Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic, had been pursuing a proof for the Navier-Stokes problem. OpenAI stated it decided to test its model after hearing researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems.

Controversies have emerged regarding the interaction between OpenAI and the researchers:

  • Collaboration offers: Buckmaster alleges he was offered “unlimited compute” and the opportunity to be the sole author of OpenAI’s announcement paper if he excluded Alpöge from the work. Bubeck acknowledged offering resources to help Buckmaster complete his proof or take over the writing of OpenAI’s paper, stating that OpenAI has made similar arrangements with other mathematicians.
  • Competing interests: Bubeck stated that Alpöge’s affiliation with Anthropic was a sticking point, questioning how OpenAI could have an internal project involving an Anthropic employee.
  • Data usage: Buckmaster questioned if OpenAI benefited from his use of Codex. While OpenAI spokesperson Laurance Fauconnet categorically denied that prompts from the last two months influenced the system, the company previously acknowledged it could not rule out that data derived from product use was used to improve the model.

💡 Why it matters

The Millennium Prize problems are considered among the most formidable challenges in mathematics, with each carrying a $1 million bounty.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #NavierStokes #AIagents #MillenniumPrize

Source: OpenAI just wants to win

item.title: Researchers Establish New Bayesian Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling in Bandit Convex Optimization
item.description:
Researchers Establish New Bayesian Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling in Bandit Convex Optimization

Researchers Bakhtiari, Lattimore, and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) have established new Bayesian regret bounds for Thompson sampling (TS) applied to bandit convex optimization problems.

🔍 Overview

The study differentiates between monotone and non-monotone ridge losses in convex optimization. The researchers provide theoretical bounds on the performance of Thompson sampling under these two distinct conditions.

⚙️ Key details

The findings establish the following regret bounds:

Loss Type Bayesian Regret Bound
Monotone ridge losses $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$
Non-monotone convex ridge losses $\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt n)$

🧩 How it works

  • Monotone Case: The proof utilizes a single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy.
  • Non-Monotone Case: The researchers demonstrate that the John-ellipsoid dichotomy fails for non-monotone links via an explicit twelve-point configuration. Instead, they employ an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for “uninformative” configurations.
  • Mathematical Argument: The bound relies on a Boolean rounding argument, which posits that a 0-1 matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has a rank of at most $2r-1$.
  • Verification: The team constructed $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses, demonstrating that the cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime.

💡 Why it matters

While these bounds have been established, it remains an open question whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence observed in the monotone case can be retained for non-monotone scenarios.

#ThompsonSampling #BanditOptimization #COLT2025 #MachineLearningTheory

Source: Thompson Sampling for Non-Monotone Convex Ridge Bandits: Monotonicity Is Not Needed for Polynomial Regret

item.title: OpenAI faces new criticism over possible use of unpublished math research
item.description:
OpenAI faces new criticism over possible use of unpublished math research

OpenAI’s recent announcement of a result on non‑sofic groups has drawn fresh criticism from mathematicians who say the company may have used unpublished research in its training data.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI announced a result involving non‑sofic groups, a class of infinite mathematical structures that cannot be approximated by finite ones.
  • The result was one of ten highlighted in the company’s announcement last month.

🧩 Concerns from the research community

  • Mathematician Andreas Thom posted on Mastodon that his earlier interactions with ChatGPT might have contributed to the success.
  • Thom and colleague Gábor Kun had prior work on non‑sofic groups that OpenAI acknowledged as heavily used.
  • Thom wrote to OpenAI researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Mark Sellke (a statistician at Harvard) asking whether his conversations were part of the training data; the reply only addressed direct access, not inclusion in the broader training corpus.
  • Thom said researchers cannot reverse‑engineer OpenAI’s training pipeline, and he urged the company to disclose datasets and usage terms.

⚙️ OpenAI’s response

  • The company amended its write‑up after criticism for not initially crediting Thom and Kun.
  • In a separate statement about its Millennium Prize Navier‑Stokes solution, OpenAI said it did not see any specific user data, but added that “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de‑identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
  • OpenAI has not commented to The Verge on the latest concerns.

💡 Why it matters

  • Thom called it “ethically indefensible” for a model to improve on non‑public research and then race the same researchers to publication without consent or credit.
  • Researchers fear such practices could push mathematics toward secrecy if rumors of breakthroughs trigger competitive races with well‑resourced AI firms.
Person Role / Affiliation
Andreas Thom Mathematician (raised concerns)
Gábor Kun Mathematician (co‑author of prior work)
Sébastien Bubeck OpenAI researcher (contacted)
Mark Sellke Statistician at Harvard (contacted)
Tristan Buckmaster Mathematics professor, New York University
Levent Alpöge Anthropic researcher (collaborated with Buckmaster)

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIEthics #TrainingData

Source: Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work

item.title: OpenAI claims Navier–Stokes solution amid credit dispute with NYU and Anthropic
item.description:
OpenAI claims Navier–Stokes solution amid credit dispute with NYU and Anthropic

Today OpenAI announced that its agents have produced a proof that the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down, a result that would solve one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI announced agents solved Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.
  • The problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000.
  • Solutions carry a $1 million prize; before today only one other Millennium Problem had been solved.
  • Navier–Stokes equations describe fluid flow and it was unknown whether they could break down to an impossible state such as infinite velocity.

⚙️ Technical Details

  • The proof shows the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down.
  • It was produced with an internal OpenAI model that outperforms the Astra model released the previous week.

Model comparison

Model Note
Astra Released last week; considered impressive
Internal OpenAI model Dramatically outperforms Astra; used for Navier–Stokes proof

⚖️ Controversy

  • Accusations that OpenAI used AI‑assisted work of NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge without credit.
  • Buckmaster posted a proof of a simplified Navier–Stokes breakdown on Mastodon; he and Alpöge had worked for almost a year using publicly available models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
  • OpenAI denied that its agents accessed Buckmaster and Alpöge’s transcripts or that employees trained on those transcripts; Mark Chen reiterated the denial.
  • Buckmaster’s document describes two options presented by OpenAI employees: (1) let Buckmaster/Alpöge post their work and OpenAI post its solution the next day, or (2) collaborate on a paper that would exclude Alpöge because of his Anthropic affiliation.
  • OpenAI also stated it does not plan to claim the million‑dollar prize.

💡 Why it matters

  • Solving Navier–Stokes would settle a major open question in fluid dynamics and mathematics.
  • The approach builds on work pioneered by mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez‑Zoroa, which experts consider promising.
  • The dispute raises questions about attribution and transparency when AI models are trained on external contributions.

#OpenAI #NavierStokes #MillenniumPrize #AIethics

Source: What OpenAI’s latest controversy tells us about the future of math
